  • Audi is slicing its bread thin when it comes to three-row performance SUVs.
  • In a recent development, our expert editors test every vehicle we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that every SQ7 comes with Audi’s familiar 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 under the hood, and this version makes 90 hp more than the outgoing model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Audi is slicing its bread thin when it comes to three-row performance SUVs. Below the flagship SQ9, there’s now a 2027 Audi SQ7. It’s the SQ9’s doppelgänger, minus a few inches of length and wearing what will be a more familiar badge for longtime Audi buyers. This is the third generation of Q7 and, like before, it straddles the space between a BMW X5 and X7, or a Mercedes-Benz GLE and GLS. And thankfully, the S model marches on with a bruiser of a V-8 engine. Audi pitched it as the SUV for the “performance family,” which is a concept that may have lost a little in translation. No matter the 0–60 of your family, though, this SQ7 is more than adept at moving lots of people around in a fast, fun manner.

In a recent development, our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Recent findings suggest that every SQ7 comes with Audi’s familiar 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 under the hood, and this version makes 90 hp more than the outgoing model. The numbers come in at 590 hp and 591 lb-ft of torque, sent through the same new, rear-biased Quattro all-whee- drive system that debuted on the SQ9. Shifting is handled by a ZF eight-speed automatic transmission, and Audi claims a 3.7-second 0–60-mph time, one-tenth quicker than the bigger SQ9. When equipped with optional summer rubber, the SQ7 tops out at a limited 155 mph.

Transmission: Eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive.

EPA MPG: 15/20/17 mpg (city/highway/combined).

According to recent reports, the TL;DR summary? Refer to my Audi SQ9 review from last month. The dynamic experience of both cars is overwhelmingly similar. But there are some small but significant differences which are worth exploring in more depth.

Like the SQ9, the SQ7 offers an optional Sport adaptive air suspension that lowers the ride height by 0.6 inch, fits more aggressive anti-roll bars, and tweaks the tune of the adaptive dampers and air suspension. While the SQ9 I drove was not fitted with this suspension, the SQ7 I tested was.

Industry observers note that as advertised, this optional suspension is indeed more dynamic than the standard setup. The significant SUV went from, sure, you can drive it hard if you want, to, this thing is actually kind of fun. Of course, the 5.5-inch shorter wheelbase, a near-nine-inch reduction in overall length, and the 100-pound diet compared to the SQ9 does some heavy lifting here too. On the Sport setup, the SQ7 turned in more swiftly and benefited from notably improved body control. Plus, power distribution is clearly more pronounced from the back axle than it is in the standard Q7 on account of the heavily rear-biased Quattro system shared with the SQ9. It’s still not as rigid or as hardcore as an X7 M60 or an AMG GLE 63 S, but Audi is moving in that direction with its sportier tune.

According to recent reports, the SQ7 makes its V-8 soundtrack known to a slightly more obvious degree than the SQ9 too. This could be down to my slightly closer proximity to the quad-tipped exhaust from the driver’s seat, or minor improvements in sound deadening, but whatever the reason, it’s improved. The V-8 rumble and meaty rip to its 7000-rpm redline were like a luxurious dessert I never tired of taking bites out of. The new SQ7’s raw pace is improved over the outgoing model, with the extra 90 horses over the previous SQ7 obvious whenever I pushed.

Fuel economy is the massive loser here. I looked down after 100 miles of California canyon road driving and noticed the trip computer readout stating 11.4 mpg. More typical driving will be better at 17 mpg combined, per the EPA rating, but expect this big SUV to gulp down the premium stuff.

There’s little to no penalty in ride when you spec the firmer suspension. The difference is so minute that it took some deep concentration over similar stretches of road to discern any penalty to comfort versus the regular Q7. If anything, there’s a touch of additional flintiness to the biggest impacts, which could just as easily be the fault of the 23-inch wheels and summer tires fitted to the SQ7 compared to the 22-inch all-seasons on the Q7. Whatever the reduction in comfort may be, the drop in ride height is worth it purely from an appearance perspective. With the Midnight Green Metallic–painted body (I know, it looks black) hugging the black-painted multi-spoke wheels, the SQ7 would make for a perfect villain car in a spy thriller.

Here’s where you really need to make the tough decision between SQ7 and SQ9. Are you planning on using the third row frequently? If so, don’t pass go, head directly to the 9. If you’re just in the game for a larger SUV and might use the third row on occasion, then the SQ7 is the one to get. The major difference isn’t necessarily in the amount of space for third-row passengers, but in cargo room with the third row in place.

According to recent reports, surprisingly, legroom in the wayback is identical between the two. But clambering into remarked space was much tougher in the SQ7 thanks to a narrower crawl-through gap behind the second row (available with a standard bench or optional captain’s chairs). Once situated, life is pretty much the same in both three-row Audis. The 4.2 cubic feet of reduced cargo space in the SQ7 will make it so that you won’t be able to bring as many goodies to the picnic as an SQ9 can carry, though.

It has been revealed that from a driver’s perspective, the SQ7’s cabin is about as good as it gets in a modern Audi. The whole layout, from the screens to the center console and feature set, is identical to the SQ9 flagship, so you could consider this a junior flagship. Optional auto-opening and -closing doors can be had. The Digital Matrix LED headlights that are so astoundingly cool in the SQ9 come standard here. Bang & Olufsen 4-D sound (also optional) with exciters in the seats makes for one hell of an audio experience.

And if you like screens, Audi’s got ’em. The 11.9-inch digital cluster blends into the 14.5-inch central infotainment system, and the 12.3-inch passenger display comes standard. I wish there were more physical controls, especially for the frustrating screen-controlled air vents, but at least Audi supplies some buttons and knobs both on the steering wheel and center console.

According to recent reports, luxury accoutrements by way of unexpected or interesting material usage are plentiful. The carbon-weave trim stands out versus traditional glossy carbon fiber. Funky fabrics on the doors and contrast stitching are appropriately nice touches. Audi claims it’s trying to do better with how it presents its interiors by doing away with piano-black plastic, and while this effort is a good start, there’s still plenty to go around on the dash, steering wheel, and center console.

Sources indicate that the approximately $19,000 you’ll save on the SQ7 over the SQ9 sure is a motivating factor for picking the smaller three-row. Its slightly better driving dynamics are another good one, but again, it’s all about priorities here. An extra-large family would be better served by the larger option.

For now, BMW doesn’t offer an X5 M60 with a V-8, and the AMG price match is the inline-six PHEV GLE 53. In other words, this gas-powered V-8 performance SUV has a little niche of its own for the time being. A Porsche Cayenne S is considerably more expensive to start, and the gap only widens when the option book comes into play.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot going for this latest generation of Audi’s smaller three-row, and outside of some small digital quirks you need to get over, it talks a persuasive game. Audi nailed the powertrain with this V-8 and its rear-biased Quattro system. And despite the SQ7’s sporty potential, there’s little compromise when it comes to usability here. The styling is arguably a bit soft in spots, but it has far more attitude than the brand’s electric offerings thanks to an upright face and pronounced fender flares.

Sources indicate that the rear-wheel steering does an excellent job of making the SQ7 drive smaller than it should. It comes standard and can turn the rear wheels up to five degrees in the opposite direction to tighten the turning radius or make the SUV dive into corners with the eagerness you’d expect from a much smaller vehicle. This, combined with lighter-than-typical and progressive steering from Audi, removed that sensation of excessive size from the driver’s seat.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Correcting yourself while parking isn't an abnormal event.
  • Because that's how many times one Chinese EV was caught on security camera footage trying to find the perfect parking spot overnight.
  • An apparently empty Avatr EV was caught on camera spending the majority of the night maneuvering around marked parking spaces in a parking structure in China's Anhui Province.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Correcting yourself while parking isn't an abnormal event. Maybe you overshot the turn and pulled just a little bit too close to the car next to you. So you back out, adjust, and try again. It's not all that embarrassing—at least not the first time. But how many times does it have to happen before you start to go red in the face (or just give up and drive away)?

Two? Five? What about 868? Because that's how many times one Chinese EV was caught on security camera footage trying to find the perfect parking spot overnight.

An apparently empty Avatr EV was caught on camera spending the majority of the night maneuvering around marked parking spaces in a parking structure in China's Anhui Province. The car can be seen on video moving around a small area of the garage. Reversing into a space, pulling forward, repositioning, and doing it all over again.

Industry observers note that watching the footage is a bit confusing. If you know that it's a car with parking assist or other autonomy features, you probably assume that the car is just having trouble deciding how well it's parked—like it's some sort of programming error that makes the car's software lack confidence that its parking job is good enough. That may not have been the case here.

It turns out that this particular car wasn't alone in its parking shenanigans. In fact, other video footage soon emerged showing other Avatr and Huajing-branded cars pulling off similar parking stunts.

While the exact reasoning for the repeated parking is unknown, CarNewsChina promptly put together that the cars in the videos all sport Huawei's driver assistance software.

In a recent development, the footage emerged just as a contest run by Huawei was taking place. It ran through November 13th and was meant to show off the capabilities of the tech company's Qiankun Intelligent Driving system by giving people points in eight different categories depending on how they used vehicles' Qiankun-backed features while driving.

One of these categories is called "Parking Elite." It measures the use of Automatic Parking Assist, Exit-and-Park Assist, Parking Lot Navigation Assist, and Remote Parking Assist to assign points to drivers. The top 100 drivers would receive Huawei points, which can be redeemed for in-app purchases and discounts.

Recent findings suggest that of course, this reportedly led to some drivers attempting to game the system. CarNewsChina even surfaces a post where one driver claims to have completed 1,000 parking sessions in a single day. It's worth noting that Huawei's tech is technically a driver-assistance feature and not an autonomous driving function; the car is supposed to always have a human supervising these types of actions.

These are just theories, of course, but the claims from drivers and security camera footage do seem like gaming the system is a plausible explanation.

Either way, you have to admit that if you saw a car parking itself 868 times overnight into various parking spaces, you'd wonder what was going on—I know I would. At least it's good for a laugh and didn't cause a traffic jam.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.
  • However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.
  • It has been revealed that the December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the latest year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield Studios is seemingly trying something different with Battlefield 6’s next patch, which everyone assumed would be a standard, mid-season update not intended to change the game significantly.

However, it appears that it may bring more to the game than we realised, enough that the developer sees it as an excuse to bring back the pre-launch Battlefield Labs testing initiative.

It has been revealed that the December 9 patch kicks off the final phase of the game’s first season, which is set to take the game through the holidays and into the latest year. We’ve known about its content for a while, and it’s definitely the lightest, compared to the two previous phases.

Battlefield Studios announced a host of new changes that will be included in the same patch, which are apparently significant enough to require player testing. The developer is reviving Battlefield Labs to help it do so, but only for three two-hour sessions, split across the game’s three main server regions (EU, NA, APAC).

Sources indicate that all tests are scheduled for today, December 2, and they remain under NDA. Battlefield Labs is also sticking with PC as its chosen platform yet again, though you will be able to join through Steam this time, alongside the EA app.

Sources indicate that the focus of the test will be on three key areas that the December 9 patch will be touching. First, there’s footstep audio, an issue that was really brought into focus with the launch of Redsec Battle Royale. You can expect to hear enemy footsteps from farther away, and intuitively know the type of surface they’re moving on.

In a recent development, the patch also brings another pass to hit registration and netcode, which BF Studios says should improve responsiveness in close-quarter situations. Finally, there are broader changes to other combat areas that the announcement didn’t elaborate on.

All testing will take place on Eastwood, and Operation Firestorm, rotating between Conquest, and Escalation.

Sources indicate that going forward, Battlefield Studios said to expect Labs to be open to more players, and for the process itself to be smoother. The developer wants to have faster turnaround times, after all, so that the initiative can test smaller changes and be more responsive to player feedback.

Recent findings suggest that some of the more involved, future sessions will include experiments with map layout changes and various other non-standard compositions of player and vehicle numbers. Of course, you can also expect fresh maps and modes to be tested in Labs, similar to how the CTE was used in Battlefield 4’s long life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tesla is rolling out the 15th iteration of its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, and the update comes with some pretty impressive graphics. It’s called Tesla Reality View, and it’s exactly that, using the vehicle’s cameras to record what’s going on around you, then re-create the scene on the central screen accurately.

The intent is to show a visual representation of what the latest FSD driver assistance is going to do, as represented by onscreen arrows. Turns are represented, and the screen reveals what parking spot the vehicle has selected when using auto park.

In a recent development, it all looks extremely slick, just like the real world rendered into a video game in real time. Tesla indicates the actual driving assistance has also been greatly improved, with an increased ability to spot and react to potholes, small animals, and road debris. The system also uses fleet learning from the trips other Teslas take on the same route, something Tesla has been doing for several iterations of FSD.

See all results for used Tesla for sale near 22546.

Although Tesla claims that this upcoming iteration is 25 times safer in critical interventions, this claim isn’t backed up with provided data such as miles driven; it’s just Tesla’s claim thus far.

Users’ experiences since the rollout have indicated that V15 appears to be more cautious in certain situations, and in some cases a little overcautious. Posts on Reddit’s Tesla forum report a vehicle aggressively avoiding random items in the road and reacting to a road repair site as if it was a pothole. Other forum users point out that early FSD updates often are a little shaky right at rollout but more polished by the time the release goes out more broadly.

It has been revealed that our own experience with Tesla’s FSD is that it works flawlessly—right up until it doesn’t and the driver needs to take over. Tesla’s own literature notes that drivers are expected to keep their attention on the road. The pretty latest graphics look attractive, but if you’re staring at the screen instead of out the windshield, FSD should theoretically automatically disconnect.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ford’s return to the top class of the 24 Hours of Le Mans was finally unveiled during the Thanksgiving Day NFL game between the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, along with an official name that clearly evokes the manufacturer’s past success: GT41.

Of course, there weren’t 39 cars before the GT40, as that name comes from the fact that the car was 40 inches tall. The GT41, for what it’s worth is 41 inches tall… almost. Technically, the car is 41.7 inches from the ground to the top of its air intake, a dimension dictated by the current FIA regulations for the LMDh class. But GT42 doesn’t quite have the same ring to it.

And while the GT41 is based off the same Oreca chassis as used by the Genesis GMR-001 and outgoing Alpine A424 and Acura ARX-06, the car and team is a wholly internal Ford effort. “Everything that we’re building, it’s in-house,” stated Mark Rushbrook, global director of Ford Racing, “It's the design, the engineering, the development, all the technical elements of the car.”.

According to recent reports, that internal approach particularly applies to the engine, which Rushbrook calls the heart of the car. The naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V-8 is based off Ford’s production engines, so much so that the block is shared with the supercharged 5.2-liter in the Mustang Dark Horse SC and F-150 Raptor R and is pulled straight from the line at the Essex Engine Plant in Windsor, Ontario. Assembled inside Ford’s dyno lab at the manufacturer’s headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, every part inside the racing engine “is designed by a Ford engineer,” according to Joseph Hendrickson, motorsports powertrain calibration engineer. “The engines are also tested on a dynamometer inside the same building. It’s a huge point of pride for us,” he stated.

Recent findings suggest that the final livery of the GT41 that will race at Le Mans will be revealed closer to the start of the 2027 WEC calendar, which being at Qatar in March. The car seen here features a camouflage pattern made of the Ford Racing wordmark, with Easter eggs hidden throughout that reflect the team’s pride as an American and Detroit-based automaker; look closely, and you’ll see an American flag, a bald eagle head, the Statue of Liberty, the Spirit of Detroit, and a football.

It has been revealed that until then, testing of the GT41 continues at several tracks around the world (and, as a reminder, Ford has no intends to run in IMSA or the 24 Hours of Daytona in 2027), while its upcoming “Go Like Hell” ad campaign—directed by Zac Snyder and narrated by Matt Damon—will make regular appearances on your various screens for the rest of the year. Including this one, if you click on the video below.

In a recent development, executive Editor Mike Austin has worked as a writer, editor, and occasional video host across titles such as Car and Driver, Autoblog, Popular Mechanics, and Hemmings (plus a few more). Prior to joining Road & Track he finally put his engineering degrees to use as an EV analyst. His personal cars skew slightly oddball, including a 1991 Honda Beat, 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan, 1987 Alfa Romeo Spider, and 2007 Saab 9-3 wagon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hoYoverse just hosted a sizeable Honkai: Star Rail Special Program, revealing more than just the game’s next major update. Version 3.8 was the big highlight, of course, with the newly introduced release arriving soon, on December 16-17 depending on your server region.

Alongside showing everything coming with this next update, the developer also confirmed that 3.8 will go on for eight weeks, rather than the usual six. V3.8 is dubbed "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams", and it brings an end to the Amphoreus journey.

The story in "Memories are the Prelude to Dreams" takes place after the final battle of Amphoreus, where Constance "The Dahlia" appears to deliver a twist: the Trailblazer's memories are scattered, with many parts missing.

It has been revealed that this final quest revolves around finding them in order to piece together the mystery, and involves a return to Penacony. This memory-hunting adventure is told from the perspective of Firefly, which will also explain how she entered the dreamscape initially and met the squad.

Sources indicate that the fresh playable character is The Dahlia, whose power is linked to the the Remembrance path, which allows her to fabricate memories. Despite taking her powers from the Remembrance, The Dhalia actually follows the Path of Nihility in-game: she’s a 5-Star character who shines in teams dealing Break DMG.

The Dhalia can unleash a Gloomy Zone that causes Toughness Reduction inflicted by allies to trigger Super Break DMG, even before you break your enemies’ Weaknesses. The Dahlia can also invite one teammate to become her Dance Partner, which allows them (and her) to deal additional Super Break DMG each time they attack an enemy. If you trigger her Ultimate after picking a Dance Partner, she applies Type Weaknesses of both partners to enemies.

While The Dahlia is the only latest character appearing in this final Amphoreus enhancement, there'll be reruns aplenty, with an unusual third banner phase to make up for the extra long wait for 4.0. Appropriately for her role in the story, Firefly will make her return alongside The Dahlia in Phase 1, while Fugue and Lingsha will both have banner reruns in Phase 2, which is expected on January 7th. A bonus two-week-long Phase 3 will then begin on January 28th, seeing brief reappearances for popular returning characters Aglaea and Sunday, before things (presumably) go back to normal with the new annual update.

Something else to look forward to in 3.8 is The Chrysos Awoo Championship, which invites players to become chimera trainers and compete in team-based battles. The Remnants of Twilight event kicks off with the fresh patch, too, featuring its own set of challenges. However, HoYoverse have confirmed that there won't be an extra event during Phase 3 — but hopefully that'll give you some time to wrap up the last of the Amphoreus story content, which is longer than the previous four chapters put together.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Trump says he “protected” Elon Musk during his first term, and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” He tied it to “a certain incident” that he called “a tough incident,” but he didn’t say what it was.

Industry observers note that musk had plenty of run-ins with federal regulators between 2017 and 2021. One of them could have ended his career as a public firm CEO, and it’s our best guess.

Trump called in to CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday. That same morning, Nvidia’s board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, and in its press release it said it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” before concluding Huang posed no national security risk.

Trump argued that the US needs to “protect our geniuses.” Then he brought up Musk:.

According to recent reports, “You know, I protected Elon in my first term. Very big. Elon was protected. I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon. I love Elon. I think he’s great. You know, 80% super genius, 20% he has other problems. But I tell him that. But Elon, I protected. You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me. And, you know, a certain incident took place, which was, you know, a tough incident.”.

It has been revealed that it’s not the first time he has hinted at it. Last week, in a Fox News interview from Shenzhen, Trump noted: “I helped Elon a lot in my first term. I helped him a lot. He was in major trouble.” Back in 2024, he told CNBC he had helped Musk “when I was president,” again without details.

According to recent reports, on August 7, 2018, Musk tweeted that he was “considering taking Tesla private at $420. Funding secured.” It wasn’t. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had shown interest, but no deal or price had been agreed, and the take-private blueprint was dead within three weeks.

In a recent development, the SEC sued Musk for securities fraud on September 27, 2018. The agency didn’t only ask for a fine. It asked the court to bar Musk from serving as an officer or director of any public tech giant. That would have meant no more Elon at Tesla, which lines up with “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me” better than anything else on this list.

And then it went away fast. Two days later, the SEC revealed a settlement: Musk stayed CEO, gave up the chairman title for three years, and he and Tesla each paid $20 million, $40 million in total. Tesla added two independent directors and agreed to have a lawyer pre-approve Musk’s material tweets, but the SEC never fully enforced it. Musk didn’t admit or deny anything.

The SEC was run at the time by Jay Clayton, a Trump appointee.

There was a criminal side too. In September 2018, federal prosecutors in San Francisco opened a fraud investigation over the same tweet. It never led to charges, and the Justice Department never said publicly why.

The SEC came back in February 2019 and asked a judge to hold Musk in contempt after he tweeted Tesla production guidance without pre-approval. That one ended in April with an amended deal listing the topics he needed approval for, and no latest penalty.

In May 2020, Musk reopened the Fremont factory in defiance of Alameda County’s COVID orders and tweeted: “If anyone is arrested, I ask that it only be me.” Trump tweeted the next day that California “should let Tesla & @elonmusk open the plant, NOW.” But the county was already working toward a reopening date of May 18, and a president doesn’t control county health orders.

It has been revealed that there’s also the September 2018 Joe Rogan episode, where Musk smoked a joint on camera. NASA followed with a workplace safety review of SpaceX and Boeing, and SpaceX lives on federal contracts.

For context, Musk sat on Trump’s business advisory councils early in that first term, and quit in June 2017 when Trump pulled out of the Paris Agreement. That feels like a lifetime ago now that xAI runs its data centers on natural gas turbines.

Our money is on “funding secured.”.

Industry observers note that musk announced a take-private deal at a specific price that the other side never agreed to, and the stock jumped. It’s textbook securities fraud. The SEC asked to remove him from public company leadership, and two days later he got a $20 million fine, an insignificant amount of money for him, and lost a mostly insignificant title. For someone who’s now worth hundreds of billions, that’s a slap on the wrist.

The main remedy was supposed to be independent oversight. Tesla gave the chair to Robyn Denholm, who had been on the board since 2014, and the board has done what Musk wanted ever since: it defended his pay packages, approved new ones, and stayed quiet while the brand took damage. Denholm herself has sold tens of millions of dollars in TSLA along the way. The SEC got a governance fix on paper and nothing in practice.

Just imagine where Tesla would be if a product oriented CEO had taken over from Elon in early 2018. The company would have spent the last 6 years developing new models instead of betting the farm on autonomy. The Cybertruck almost certainly does not happen, at least not in its current form. Instead, they would have developed a more conventional pickup. We'd have gotten 2nd generation models of the X and S instead of them being canceled. Instead of a Cybercab, there would be a model 2 compact car people could buy. And there would likely be a Tesla van and a full sized SUV, possibly developed on the same underlying platform. Also, the SEC was trying to ban him from running public companies. At the time, SpaceX was still private. So, Elon could have still run SpaceX.

Trump likes to take credit, and he could be inflating his role here. But if the White House leaned on the SEC or the Justice Department in 2018 to help a CEO facing fraud allegations, that’s a serious problem, and someone should look into it.

The timing doesn’t help. He noted it the same day he appears to have intervened to reinstate Huang as CEO of Nvidia.

So what exactly did the administration do in 2018, and what does Musk owe for it?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you ask the auto industry, subscriptions are the future.
  • A new law aims to put a stop to many forms of in-car subscriptions and after-sale purchases, meaning that if all it takes is a credit card number to switch on a feature after you buy the car, it probably isn't going to fly in New York State.
  • It has been revealed that governor Kathy Hochul signed into law a bill that prohibits automakers, dealerships, and third-party providers from charging car buyers ongoing subscription fees in certain cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you ask the auto industry, subscriptions are the future. Consumers might disagree. They don't want basic features like heated seats being locked behind a paywall, especially when the hardware is already installed. Legislators in New York have decided those types of subscriptions are nothing more than a money grab.

A new law aims to put a stop to many forms of in-car subscriptions and after-sale purchases, meaning that if all it takes is a credit card number to switch on a feature after you buy the car, it probably isn't going to fly in New York State. But there are, of course, some exclusions.

It has been revealed that governor Kathy Hochul signed into law a bill that prohibits automakers, dealerships, and third-party providers from charging car buyers ongoing subscription fees in certain cases. Specifically, it prohibits recurring fees for hardware already installed in the car at the time of purchase, so long as those features don't create an ongoing cost for the manufacturer or a provider.

A snippet from the State's announcement says it best (and uses the infamous heated seat subscription as a prime example):.

Amid rising consumer prices, the latest law guards against a rising trend of car companies charging car owners fees to activate and use built-in features like heated seats, enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.

There are, of course, provisions in the legislation of what features aren't covered by the subscription freeze.

New York says that driver assistance and automation features, connected cellular services, in-car hotspot, satellite radio, vehicle telematics, roadside assistance, navigation updates, and infotainment features are some of the items excluded from protection under the new legislation.

Sources indicate that notably, that means Tesla can continue charging for features like Full Self-Driving. It does, however, call into question features like Acceleration Boost, which is a $2,000 software-based performance upgrade that requires no extra ongoing costs.

This distinction tracks fairly in line with what both enthusiasts and consumers have been shouting at their phone screens for the last few years. If it's local hardware that's already installed in the vehicle and requires no ongoing costs to maintain (like heated seats, climate control, or remote start using a physical key fob), it feels like a cash grab to continue to charge owners after purchasing the vehicle. Things that cost money to provide—like internet-connected streaming features or driver assistance features that are being actively developed and upgraded over the air—are a bit more defensible.

Industry observers note that if your $70,000 SUV still needs its manufacturer's servers, cellular network, fresh maps with to-the-minute traffic conditions, and continuously updated self-driving software—you might not get out of paying a monthly fee. But if it just needs a relay flipped on to work completely offline, then the manufacturer better just work it into the cost.

“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover,” the court mentioned in its November 20 ruling, AN reported. “The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”.

The Defender is JLR’s best-selling vehicle globally, with the automaker shipping more than 100,000 units last year. Both vehicles have boxy designs with flat rooflights, squared wheel arches, and, notably, body-colored panels in place of the rear side windows.

In a recent development, unfortunately for JLR, the judge also ruled that the court does not have authority over BYD’s U.K. arm. To that end, JLR is reportedly planning to bring the same claim to the courts in England.

Sources indicate that according to AN, BYD “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and has plans to appeal the result. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights,” the company stated. “We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect.”.

While the final ruling will likely take some time before it is unveiled, the Dutch court has prohibited BYD from producing the Ti7 at its new factory in Hungary, where it was due to begin mass production early next year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the first fully electric Porsche Boxster is finally in the home stretch of development. Ahead of its official debut in early 2027, Porsche offered an early look at the two-door electric sports car.

Despite rumors that the all-electric 718 Boxster was canceled, Porsche confirmed on Tuesday that the Boxster EV will debut in the first quarter of 2027.

“Starting next year, the all-electric 718 Boxster will offer our customers a compelling entry point into the world of two-door sports cars,” Porsche CEO Dr Michael Leiters mentioned.

Ahead of its upcoming debut, Porsche is putting the electric sports car through the paces to ensure it preserves the DNA of its predecessors, a top priority.

Porsche developed a fresh “E-Core” architecture specifically for the 718 Boxster to lower the seat position and optimize weight distribution.

According to recent reports, with the 800-volt battery mounted directly behind the seats, where the internal combustion engine would typically be found, the weight is concentrated toward the middle of the vehicle. The electric Boxster has a weight distribution of 40% on the front axle and 60% on the rear, matching that of a traditional mid-engined sports car.

It also features an “intelligent lightweight construction,” as Porsche calls it, so the vehicle’s overall weight matches that of the current 911 Cabriolet models with its T-Hybrid powertrain.

“Our engineers have succeeded in transferring the Boxster’s unique concept to the electric world, further enhancing it in the process,” Porsche’s CEO mentioned.

The electric Boxster shares many chassis components with the 911, including the steering, which is based on the 911 Carrera GTS. It will offer rear-axle steering, a first for the 718 Boxster.

Meanwhile, the wheel and tire dimensions and braking system are based on the Porsche 911, and the electronically controlled PTV+ limited-slip differential is also pulled from the 911.

Porsche remarked the electric Boxster will be “the most powerful 718 ever,” but didn’t offer a specific output figure.

The range-topping Boxster EV can sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in under three seconds, according to Porsche, and it can reach a top speed of over 155 mph (250 km/h).

Sources indicate that all electric Boxster models will be RWD and come standard with E-Shift. Like Hyundai’s performance N EVs, including the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, the Porsche Boxster EV features a virtual gear shift that simulates the feeling and sounds of a seven-speed PDK transmission.

When E-Shift mode is not active, the paddle can be used to toggle between three levels of recuperation.

The electric Porsche 718 Boxster will make its official debut in the first quarter of 2027, so we should learn more details soon. IT will be built at Porsche’s main plant in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen, Germany.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that battlefield 6 is about to receive a fresh revision.
  • That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.
  • In a recent development, thew latest content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that battlefield 6 is about to receive a fresh revision. Version 1.1.3.0 is set to arrive tomorrow, December 9 to kick off the third and final phase of the game’s first season. Winter Offensive brings some holiday-themed new content to the game, but it’s not the most interesting part of the patch.

That honour goes to a couple of the high-level changes Battlefield Studios has included with the new patch, which range from a major pass on audio to a fix for a particularly annoying bug that’s been seemingly introduced with a recent patch.

In a recent development, thew latest content takes the form of a limited-time version of the game’s Empire State map, which covers it in snow and tweaks its layout slightly. To go along with that there are new limited-time modes for both multiplayer and Redsec’s Gauntlet. The event mode will be available in Conquest, and Domination.

According to recent reports, the Ice Climbing Axe is the only fresh weapon in this drop. The battle pass gets a new Winter Offensive bonus path, just like we’ve seen with previous seasonal stages. This is how you unlock the axe, too.

Easily the most interesting change in this update is the range of improvements to audio across the board. First, footstep audio received a big pass that should make it easier to hear enemy footsteps, easier to locate them, and across different surfaces.

Some of the bugs that caused certain sounds to simply vanish have been fixed. This was especially prevalent in battle royale matches. BF Studios explained in the patch notes that it has adjusted memory priorities for in-game sounds in order to prioritise the most crucial ones. This is not the end of the road on audio, however, as the developer continues to work on making the soundscape more stable and reliable.

Some of those audio changes are the result of recent testing done in Battlefield Labs, which is also responsible for another exciting addition in this latest patch: improvements to hit registration.

While BF6 has had solid and stable netcode, certain situations would sometimes create uncertainty about how you died, and why certain actions seemingly failed to perform at that particular moment.

The focus in this upgrade is to improve the reliability of how actions in close-quarter combat are translated, which includes firing before fully going into ADS, quick aim changes and more.

According to recent reports, speaking of close-range, the patch also brings another pass to soldier visibility to make it easier for enemies to stand out from the background. This is particularly relevant in areas with low contrast, or busy environments with lots of particle and visual effects.

1.1.3.0 also brings yet another set of weapon handling and gunplay tweaks, this time focusing on accuracy issues with first shots. You can also expect more tweaks to attachment behaviour with regards to recoil.

Something else worth highlighting is that vehicle gameplay is getting several smaller tweaks that have to do with how they interact with the world, how their HUDs behave and more. Finally, your settings should no longer be reset after applying an patch. BF Studios states there are still some instances where that might happen, but the glitch should be fixed for the majority of players.

You can read the full change log on the Battlefield blog.

#168209. Tested: The 2028 Volvo XC60 T8 Is the Rangiest Plug-In Hybrid

Tested: The 2028 Volvo XC60 T8 Is the Rangiest Plug-In Hybrid

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the journey to the future of automotive propulsion, Volvo was an early adopter of the all-electric ethos.
  • Our expert editors test every vehicle we review.
  • We have always appreciated the charms of the current-generation XC60, with a substantial package of changes sharpening its case for a few more years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the journey to the future of automotive propulsion, Volvo was an early adopter of the all-electric ethos. The Swedish automaker initially vowed to stop selling all gasoline-powered cars—including hybrids—by 2030. A few years and three newly introduced all-electric models later, Volvo has radically altered that plan and will continue to sell hybrid models past that point. That includes extending the life of the existing lineup, with the already-near-decade-old second-gen XC60 getting a new T8 powertrain, which gives it the longest pure electric range of any plug-in hybrid on sale in the U.S.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

We have always appreciated the charms of the current-generation XC60, with a substantial package of changes sharpening its case for a few more years. Visually, the most obvious changes are a new front end incorporating LED matrix headlights and smaller revisions at the rear. The technical highlight is an improved 78-mile EPA electric range from a mammoth 37.9-kWh battery pack, this delivered to a motor on the rear axle; a smaller starter-generator can add modest assistance at the front as well. Volvo quotes a peak electric output of 208 hp, with the 2.0-liter turbo four that drives the front wheels able to deliver 247 horses. Inside, the XC60 receives small material and trim adjustments.

Engine: 1969-cc turbocharged inline-four, hybridized.

Power: 455 hp (peak system output).

Torque: 494 lb-ft (peak system output).

Transmission: eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive.

As I pulled into Copenhagen’s morning traffic, Volvo’s Pure drive mode, which idles the gasoline-powered engine in favor of an all-electric experience, felt prudent among the multitude of commuting bicyclists. Silent running was entirely suited to the Scandinavian environment, but the XC60 T8 wasn’t stumbling over itself either when running under electrical power, Volvo having significantly juiced up the electric motor alongside the bigger battery pack.

While 208 hp in Pure EV mode has to work against 4855 pounds of weight, the T8 felt well suited to both metropolitan driving and the open road, the effective surge of electrical power proving itself on highways and the 9.9-mile-long Øresund Link that connects Denmark to Malmö, Sweden. Power delivery definitely wasn’t as aggressive as that of a spicy EV, but it wasn’t gentle either, and the electric motor had enough punch to drive the XC60 without me yearning for the gas engine to intervene. Something that won’t happen unless the accelerator is pushed to a kickdown position or by switching drive modes. The 78-mile EPA range is genuinely class-leading, and selecting the T8’s Charge mode rapidly replenished e-miles when selected.

Switching from the Pure to Hybrid mode was where the real fun began. And fun isn’t too strong a word for the unlikely performance of the split hybrid system as the 2.0-liter turbo adds its contribution to the front axle, giving a combined peak of 455 hp and what Volvo claims is 4.5-second 0–60-mph capability. In practice, the XC60 T8 felt shockingly quick, rapidly spinning up the speedometer at wide-open throttle. The accelerator has a two-part action, with softer response at the top of its travel metering electrical power before the combustion horses arrive with a suddenness. This was fun, but the transition also felt a bit too obvious considering how subtle some hybrids now are. Switching it up to Power mode refocused the powertrain by keeping the engine running and solved the on-and-off drama. The eight-speed automatic transmission shifts without drama, and there’s enough electrical torque that I didn’t even want for the missing steering-wheel paddle shifters.

We liked the way the pre-facelift XC60 T8 drove, and the newly introduced version impressed as much. Volvos are traditionally heavy and somewhat leisurely to respond, but the XC60 successfully belied its scale with impressively neutral handling on narrow Swedish country roads. My XC60 test vehicle was fitted with the optional air suspension and active shock absorbers, fighting body roll and delivering a reactive front end.

Industry observers note that similarly, Volvo’s power-steering system was smooth and direct, though both weight settings skewed overly light for my tastes. It’s not as overtly sporty as some performance SUVs, but its combination of qualities was definitely appealing. My only complaints were a somewhat agricultural soundtrack under full throttle and what was often a harsh ride over rough surfaces, bumps, and imperfections being transferred into the cabin.

It has been revealed that I didn’t get a chance to plug in the XC60, but Volvo said the 2028 model can charge at speeds up to 7.2 kWh. All told, the XC60 PHEV will take around 5.7 hours to fully charge up at maximum speed.

Industry observers note that volvo has long succeeded at creating minimalist cabins without them looking sparse or cheap, and the XC60 continues to carry that torch with a few exceptions. And one of these exceptions was the 11.2-inch center touchscreen, which has been blown out of the casing found on previous model years to take over the entire console.

Annoyingly, climate-control functions are integrated into this display with multiple menus required for adjustment, the Android Auto software beneath it starting to show its age. Similarly, Apple CarPlay is only available through a wired connection—that’s so 2017. That said, the infotainment system was easy to operate despite its limitations. Plus, Volvo has perfected the art of displaying turn-by-turn directions on the instrument cluster; a dial speedometer and tachometer sit opposite each other with an appropriately scaled navigation map centered in between.

Beyond the technology, the XC60’s interior was a charming place to spend time. Fresh Scandinavian-inspired materials on the dashboard included brushed wood and knit fabric, which looked upmarket and were pleasing to the touch. The light leather seats were firm yet comfortable and included massage, heating, and cooling functions, which can be operated all at once. Other notable interior design wins include a wooden sliding cup-holder cover, an alluring crystal shift knob, and satisfying brushed steel door handles. The Bowers & Wilkins stereo system on my test car was fantastic, and Volvo deserves points for retaining a traditional volume knob, as well as tactile buttons to skip songs.

If you want a properly long-range plug-in hybrid SUV, the Volvo XC60 may be your best option, at least for now. The next longest-range mid-size luxury SUV option is the Mercedes-Benz GLC Hybrid, which offers 54 all-electric miles. Toyota also offers a RAV4 Plug-In Hybrid with 52 miles of range. Volvo has not announced finalized U.S. pricing for the 2028 XC60 T8 yet.

In a recent development, volvo interiors are well known for minimalist luxury, but even the Swedes can’t help themselves from including an easter egg here and there. Placed on the right edge of the passenger-side dashboard, Volvo has engraved a miniature Swedish flag on the brushed aluminum trim.

#168208. Here’s How To Make Your Holiday EV Road Trip Easier

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1092 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Insideevs ↗ Open Full Page

Here’s How To Make Your Holiday EV Road Trip Easier

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a short workweek for most of us here in the United States.
  • Here are a few tips that can take the edge off a long trip.
  • DC fast charging times are getting better and better, but charging still takes longer than stopping for gas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a short workweek for most of us here in the United States. In just a day or two, many of us will load up our cars and trek around the country to our loved ones. If you’re reading this, there’s a decent chance you’ll be taking on of those trips in an electric vehicle. EVs have come a long way, so in theory, range anxiety shouldn’t be much of an issue for anyone these days. Still, with so many drivers on the roads, there are bound to be annoyances that come with long EV road trips.

Here are a few tips that can take the edge off a long trip.

DC fast charging times are getting better and better, but charging still takes longer than stopping for gas. Thus, bottlenecks can occur on well-traveled routes with limited DC fast charging stops. It’s just kind of the nature of the beast when most people are stopping for 20-30 minutes. Multiply that by the plethora of drivers also trying to charge up and get home, and well, it’s not hard to see why EV charging queues can balloon, adding time to your drive home.

Recent findings suggest that but you can head some of that off if you prep the night before. For those with home charging, that means simply plugging the car in and ensuring it’s fully charged for the next day’s trip. For those who don’t have access to home charging, using a DC fast charger the night before, when everyone isn’t rushing to leave, could ease some of the frustration of charging up before getting on the roads.

Sources indicate that also, some DC fast charging companies give a discount for charging during off-peak hours. Prepping the night before won’t just save you time, it might save you money.

Sources indicate that we may have a set route in mind for our trip, and that could be all fine and dandy, but is it really the best route for our cars? Electric vehicles tend to consume more energy at higher speeds and when traveling up hills. Thus, it could be advantageous to maximize range by picking a flatter route, or one with lower speeds.

In most cases this won’t be necessary, but if you’re pushing the limits of your car and the infrastructure around you, it’s good to know. Most route planning apps—like A Better Route Planner, Plugshare, or even Google Maps—take into account which route is friendlier to your car’s range calculator, and may suggest detours if you get a big range boost from a route that’s nearly as quick.

Industry observers note that these route planners will tell you exactly when and where to stop, depending on your car’s efficiency, your destination, your desired state of charge at arrival, and road conditions along the way. They can be adjusted to fit your real-world efficiency data or your need for breaks. Rather than just winging, using a route planner ensures you’re never in an uncomfortable situation without the range or charging ability to get where you need to go.

This goes hand in hand with route planning, but I think it is relevant here. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest travel day of the year. You’re not the only one on the road who will need charging. Prepping the night before can help with the initial charging wait times at the start of your trip. If you’re on a long journey, chances are you’ll find yourself in a big queue at a strange charger.

Industry observers note that when you’re planning your route with charging stops, pay attention to what brands they are and what ports they use. An increasing number of highway stops often have several competing charging stations. A Tesla Supercharging station could have an Ionna Rechargery nearby. Or maybe it’s an EV Go station. Or maybe it’s a charging station by Circle K or Shell. In any case, they tend to cluster together near high-power infrastructure. Rather than fumble with apps and payments at the station, I think it’s best if you research the charging companies on your route and pre-emptively install their apps and set up payment.

In a recent development, similarly, bring an adapter. NACS is promptly making its way across the country, but not every station has NACS ports, and not every one has CCS. Some of the stations with your desired plug will likely be busy. An adapter that allows your car to access both NACS and CCS ports will save a lot of headaches.

Once again, you’re not the only one trying to get home for the holidays. Let’s keep the queue moving, and try not to charge more than 80%, if possible. Charging speeds slow substantially when EV batteries surpass 80%. It may have only taken 15-20 minutes to get to 80%, but it’ll take another 20 or so to reach 100%, or much longer in some cars. Chances are, there’s someone waiting. Not only is it courteous to unplug and move on, but it’s also probably quicker to charge again (if you need it) closer to your destination.

I know this list has mostly been about minimizing time lost due to charging, but I think it’s key to remember that it’s okay to take a break. Charging stops are inherently longer than refuelling a gas car, but I think that 15-30 minute break is helpful for safe driving. Taking a rest, using the restroom, or getting a snack can take the edge off a trip. Use an EV’s characteristics to your advantage.

I’ve been doing EV road trips since 2021, and it’s amazing to see just how far both vehicle range and charging infrastructure have come. Long trips are possible for most drivers these days, whereas years ago, it was a huge hardship or even impossible. With better apps, better infrastructure, and better cars, it’s only gotten easier. But it still pays to know what you’re doing. Drive safely out there, folks.

#168207. Two tech companies tried to reinvent the e-bike. Why DJI’s Amflow soared while Rivian’s ALSO floundered

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2081 w)
📖 Baca

Two tech companies tried to reinvent the e-bike. Why DJI’s Amflow soared while Rivian’s ALSO floundered

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two of the most interesting upcoming electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.
  • According to recent reports, amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just debuted its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim.
  • Both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two of the most interesting upcoming electric bicycle companies in the world made headlines on the same day last week, and for two very different reasons.

According to recent reports, amflow, the electric bicycle brand that emerged from the same engineering ecosystem responsible for DJI’s revolutionary Avinox drive system, just debuted its first commuter e-bike to widespread acclaim. Meanwhile, ALSO, the high-tech electric bicycle startup spun out of Rivian, declared that it was halting deliveries of its futuristic TM-B electric bicycle amid mounting software problems.

Both companies set out to build something arguably similar: a premium, high-performance electric bicycle that uses sophisticated technology to make riding easier, more enjoyable, and more practical. Both have deep engineering roots and were incubated by successful technology companies. And both have developed impressive proprietary systems that set their bikes apart from the competition.

But their dramatically different launches offer an interesting lesson about the difference between innovation and execution, and which has proven to be more successful in the real world.

Amflow’s story actually begins before the brand released its first electric mountain bike.

DJI, the Chinese drone giant, had spent years perfecting the art of building small, lightweight, powerful electric motors, sophisticated electronic controllers, and advanced battery management systems. Those are all technologies that translate remarkably well to electric bicycles, even if the applications are quite different.

Sources indicate that that expertise helped give rise to the Avinox e-bike drive system, which rapidly earned a reputation as one of the most impressive electric bicycle drivetrains on the market. The mid-drive motor and control system rapidly ate away at the huge market share long held by Bosch and other leaders.

Recent findings suggest that the motors offered an almost ridiculous amount of power in a lightweight package, paired with sophisticated sensors and software that delivered smooth, natural-feeling pedal assistance. The system was also designed as a tightly integrated ecosystem, with displays, controllers, batteries, and motors working together.

Amflow’s first electric mountain bikes demonstrated just how well that technology could work in the real world.

And now, with the launch of the new Amflow UE commuter series, the organization is taking that proven technology and applying it to an entirely different kind of riding.

The new bikes bring Avinox’s powerful pedal assistance and intelligent electronic controls to a more practical urban platform, adding commuter-focused features designed to make everyday riding more convenient.

There’s plenty of proprietary technology here, but perhaps the most important thing about Amflow’s approach is what the company didn’t reinvent.

The bikes still fundamentally work like bicycles.

Industry observers note that you pedal, a conventional mechanical drivetrain transfers that power to the rear wheel, and an electric motor provides assistance. It’s the same basic arrangement that has worked on electric bicycles for decades, just refined with much more advanced engineering.

Sources indicate that amflow didn’t need to fundamentally change the bicycle to make it feel futuristic. Instead, the organization focused on making the familiar bicycle experience better.

And while the new commuter models are still too fresh to judge their long-term reliability, early impressions have been overwhelmingly positive. That’s an encouraging start, especially considering the company’s already established reputation in the demanding electric mountain bike market.

ALSO, on the other hand, took a dramatically different approach.

The company emerged from Rivian, the American electric vehicle manufacturer known for its technologically advanced electric trucks and SUVs.

Like DJI, Rivian has extensive experience developing sophisticated electric drivetrains, battery systems, power electronics, and software. And like Amflow, ALSO wanted to bring that expertise to a new generation of electric bicycles.

But instead of using those technologies to improve a conventional bicycle, ALSO decided to rethink the entire machine.

The firm’s TM-B electric bicycle uses a pedal-by-wire system, meaning the pedals aren’t mechanically connected to the rear wheel. Instead, pedaling turns a generator that sends data signals and power through an electronic system, while software determines how the rear motor responds.

According to recent reports, pedal-by-wire systems have some genuine potential advantages. They can eliminate traditional chains, belts, derailleurs, and other mechanical drivetrain components, which has helped land them on many unconventional e-bikes such as extremely long cargo e-bikes and truck-like electric bicycles that would otherwise require ridiculously long chain runs.

They can also allow engineers to completely customize the relationship between pedaling effort and motor response, creating riding experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a conventional bicycle drivetrain.

In a recent development, but there’s a catch. When you replace a relatively simple mechanical system with a sophisticated electronic one, you’re also introducing a lot more opportunities for things to go wrong.

And unlike a conventional bicycle, where many drivetrain problems can be diagnosed and repaired with basic tools, a highly proprietary software-defined bicycle can become much more dependent on its manufacturer to keep it running.

That’s not inherently a bad tradeoff. Modern electric cars have demonstrated that software-defined vehicles can offer tremendous benefits. But it puts enormous pressure on the manufacturer to get the hardware, software, and integration right.

Unfortunately, ALSO’s early rollout suggests that the company hasn’t quite managed that yet.

The contrast between the two companies became particularly striking last week.

Amflow unveiled its new commuter models, building on the reputation of its successful electric mountain bikes and earning enthusiastic early reviews.

ALSO, meanwhile, confirmed that it was pausing deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycle due to software-related challenges. That’s on top of earlier delivery delays and reports of customers having to send their latest ALSO TM-B bicycles back for repairs.

According to recent reports, we’ve also previously reported on some unusual charging and discharging behavior with the TM-B, raising questions about how the bike’s sophisticated electronic systems were managing energy. Those concerns now look particularly relevant in light of the company’s latest announcement.

To be fair, we don’t know how widespread the problems are across ALSO’s delivered bicycles, and it’s entirely possible that the tech giant will resolve these complications relatively rapidly with updates on delivered bikes and reflashing software on bikes yet to be shipped.

Sources indicate that nor should we assume that Amflow’s newly introduced commuter bikes will be trouble-free simply because their initial reviews are positive. Long-term reliability is something that can only be established over time. But the difference in their respective launches is hard to ignore.

Both are examples of tech-focused startups attempting to reinvent the future of e-bikes. One tech giant is expanding its lineup after successfully establishing its technology in the market. The other is struggling to get its first product consistently into customers’ hands.

And that brings us to what I think is the most interesting part of this story.

There’s a fundamental difference between developing impressive technology and successfully turning that technology into a dependable consumer product.

Both Amflow and ALSO have accomplished the first part.

The engineering behind the Avinox drive system is genuinely impressive, and the TM-B’s pedal-by-wire architecture is one of the more ambitious attempts to rethink the electric bicycle in recent years.

But Amflow appears to have taken a more measured approach to bringing that technology to consumers.

The tech giant first developed and refined a sophisticated electric bicycle drivetrain, proved it in the demanding electric mountain bike market, and then adapted it to commuter applications.

ALSO attempted something much more ambitious right out of the gate: launching an entirely newly introduced bicycle architecture with numerous interdependent proprietary systems.

In a recent development, neither approach is inherently wrong. In fact, if nobody ever attempted the latter, we’d probably miss out on some genuinely revolutionary products. But there’s a reason that so many successful technological innovations are evolutionary rather than revolutionary.

Industry observers note that sometimes the smartest engineering decision isn’t figuring out how to replace something that already works. It’s figuring out how to make it work better.

And there’s a certain irony in the fact that Amflow’s new commuter bike looks relatively ordinary, yet appears to deliver an extraordinary riding experience.

ALSO’s TM-B, meanwhile, looks like something from the future, but its early ownership experience has been considerably less impressive.

I want to be clear that I’m not rooting for or against either tech giant here.

In a recent development, quite the opposite. Both ALSO and Amflow are working to accelerate the state of the industry. I’ve been fascinated by the TM-B since it was first unveiled, and I genuinely hope the organization succeeds. And Amflow has taken the fresh perspective brought by its parent company, DJI, and turned it into real-world progress. The e-bike industry needs more innovation to help push everyone forward.

I love seeing companies take major swings in the electric bicycle industry, especially when they’re attempting something more interesting than slapping a bigger motor and battery onto an otherwise generic frame.

Industry observers note that and I think pedal-by-wire technology has real potential. The ability to electronically control the relationship between pedaling and propulsion opens up fascinating possibilities, even if it also introduces new challenges.

In a recent development, I should also mention that I have not personally ridden either of these bikes, and thus this is analysis from the sidelines. The Amflow UE Carbon was only unveiled a few days ago, though I’ve got one on the way and am excited to begin testing it soon and to report back here on the experience. As for ALSO, the bike was unveiled a year ago, and I was slated to be at the launch for test riding, but barely an hour after I posted an exclusive article revealing that ALSO had accidentally leaked its own images of its yet-to-be-unveiled bike on its website, I received an email uninviting me to the upcoming event and test ride.

So keep in mind that all of this is being remarked as an analyst with nearly two decades in the e-bike industry and hundreds of different e-bikes under my belt, not from personal experience with either bike model.

According to recent reports, but as someone who spends an enormous amount of time riding, testing, and working on electric bicycles, I also appreciate the value of simplicity. A bicycle is an inherently elegant machine. It’s lightweight, efficient, relatively easy to maintain, and remarkably dependable considering how few components it needs to function.

Sources indicate that electric assistance has already made that machine dramatically more useful for millions of people. The question is how much more complexity we should introduce in pursuit of further improvements.

Amflow seems to be asking, “How can we use advanced technology to make riding a bicycle better?”.

ALSO seems to be asking, “What if we could completely rethink how a bicycle works?”.

Sources indicate that both are worthwhile questions, and I’m glad there are companies pursuing both answers. But right now, Amflow is demonstrating the advantages of building on a proven foundation, while ALSO is learning some painful lessons about the challenges of reinventing the wheel.

It has been revealed that it's pretty clear that electric cars are much simpler than ICE cars, and I would argue this is an advantage. However, the same cannot be said for the ALSO bike. It's much more complicated than a normal bike, or even a normal e-bike. It seems like an answer in search of a problem.

And perhaps that’s the biggest takeaway from this tale of two high-tech e-bike startups.

The future of electric bicycles will undoubtedly involve more sophisticated motors, batteries, sensors, and software. But the companies that succeed won’t necessarily be the ones that pack the most technology into their bikes.

They’ll be the ones that figure out how to make all that technology work so seamlessly that riders barely have to think about it.

Because at the end of the day, the best electric bicycle isn’t necessarily the one with the most advanced technology. It’s the one that makes you want to ride it every day – and actually lets you.

This BMW iX3 Drove Over 600 Miles On One Charge. The Catch? It Took Nearly 18 Hours

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s no surprise by now that the newly introduced BMW iX3 is a great long-range electric SUV.
  • In a recent development, BMW Brazil wanted to demonstrate that the first Neue Klasse-based model can do the rather demanding trip from Brasília to São Paulo without recharging along the way.
  • Still, the crew made it, but it involved a lot of planning, a very careful right foot, and plenty of patience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s no surprise by now that the newly introduced BMW iX3 is a great long-range electric SUV. It blew past its official range rating in several tests and beat the competition in a few independent comparisons. Now, though, the iX3 is putting another performance under its belt, but it’s a whole other story whether regular drivers would actually go to all the trouble to replicate it.

In a recent development, BMW Brazil wanted to demonstrate that the first Neue Klasse-based model can do the rather demanding trip from Brasília to São Paulo without recharging along the way. That’s a 631-mile (1,016-kilometer) journey, while the iX3’s official range rating in Brazil sits at 354 miles (570 km). In the U.S., the 2027 iX3 50 xDrive, the same trim as the one put to the test in South America, has an EPA-rated 434 miles of range, so nowhere near the target distance.

Still, the crew made it, but it involved a lot of planning, a very careful right foot, and plenty of patience. Here’s how they did it.

Maximizing efficiency was the main goal, so the drivers aimed for a constant pace, avoiding busy roads, unnecessary acceleration, and steep deceleration. The iX3, which is powered by a 112-kilowatt-hour battery in the U.S., ended up traveling at speeds between 37 and 43 miles per hour (60-90 kilometers per hour), with short stints at up to 56 mph (90 kph) when the road was clear.

Industry observers note that the drivers also made full use of the Max Range mode throughout the trip, which prioritizes efficiency over performance. It’s safe to say that the car’s 469 horsepower had a pretty restful day when BMW decided to go on this trip.

In a recent development, after traveling 439 miles, the electric SUV still had 30% left in the battery, with 193 miles (312 km) of estimated range left. At 15% battery level, the car had traveled 538 miles (866 km), with 99 miles (159 km) of projected range left. The numbers mentioned the trip would be possible, so the team soldiered on, starting the final stretch at around 4 a.m. to avoid the São Paulo rush hour. In the end, the iX3 reached its destination, having covered 631 miles (1,015.8 km) on a single charge, but the time it took to check off this achievement was excruciatingly long: 17 hours and 30 minutes.

According to recent reports, the car’s trip computer highlighted an average energy consumption of 17.6 kilowatt-hours/100 miles (10.9 kWh/100 km), while the average speed was just 35.5 mph (57.1 kph). That’s good enough when the only goal is to squeeze as many miles out of the battery as possible, but there aren’t many people out there who are willing to spend so much time behind the wheel just to prove a point.

Seeing how the iX3 can charge at up to 400 kW and a 10-to-80% top-up can take as little as 21 minutes, a short charging session can make a big difference during a real-world road trip.

Still, BMW Brazil’s achievement tops that of its Chinese counterpart. Earlier this year, a Chinese-spec iX3 50L xDrive drove over 500 miles on a single charge, averaging 20.2 kWh/100 miles (12.2 kWh/100 km).

A fleet of specially equipped Lucid Gravity SUVs has also been on the prowl in the Bay Area this year, testing a self-driving ride-hailing experience for Uber. While these tests have been run with a safety driver ready to take over, the Gravity SUVs are now going fully driverless.

The modified Gravity SUVs are the product of a collaboration between Lucid, Uber, and Nuro, a manufacturer that builds autonomous driving software. The robotaxis feature an Uber-designed cabin interface and are operated by Nuro’s autonomous driving system. High-resolution cameras, lidar sensors, and radar sensors are integrated into the Gravity’s body and mounted to a rooftop “halo” that doubles as a way for riders to identify the correct vehicle through LED lights.

See all results for latest 2027 Lucid Motors Gravity for sale near 29405.

Testing first began with human supervision in the Bay Area in December 2025. Since then, Nuro has continued to conduct supervised round-the-clock testing in San Francisco and Houston. The tech giant now notes it’s ready to begin its next phase, which involves driving on public roads without a safety operator inside.

Recent findings suggest that lucid built and delivered over 100 autonomous vehicles to complete this next stage. The California Department of Motor Vehicles has issued two permits this year that allow the vehicles to test on public roads without a safety operator inside and allow for passenger rides when a safety driver is present.

As part of the collaboration’s terms, Uber has committed to owning and operating at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles equipped with Nuro’s autonomous technology. The service is expected to launch to the public in the Bay Area by early 2027, followed by releases in dozens of global markets over the next few years.

💡 Key Takeaways
