💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood.
  • The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.
  • Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A latest study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged.

The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.

Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain.

Using AI to Investigate Bone Density and Brain Health.

According to recent reports, to explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance.

Industry observers note that the researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine.

Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group.

The researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia.

Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time.

Lower Bone Density Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline.

The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance.

The researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are important for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention.

Sources indicate that another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density showed a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity.

"This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri said. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration.".

Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia.

Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging.

In a recent development, "This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri remarked. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect.".

These findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health.

Routine CT Scans Could Reveal Hidden Signs of Brain Aging.

One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons.

Recent findings suggest that "Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh said. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function.".

By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together.

Dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms.".

Industry observers note that the study highlights a potentially important connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain.

Sources indicate that the study, "Deep Learning-derived Bone Mineral Density and Longitudinal White Matter Microstructure and Cognitive Decline: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis," also included Quincy A.   • The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan.
  • Sources indicate that A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that suzuki left the U.S. car market in 2012, but it still builds the kind of small hatchbacks European buyers have long favored, now also powered by electricity. Its latest is the Ignis EV, a city car that measures just 11 feet 9 inches long (3.57 meters). It’s due in Europe in summer 2027, when it will face a upcoming generation of small EVs from both European and Chinese automakers.

The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan. The firm recently launched the e Sky there, an electric kei car that supplies the basis for the Ignis’s body and powertrain. The Ignis still has the typical kei proportions (it's tall and narrow), but Suzuki claims it took the car onto European city streets and winding roads to tune the suspension and power delivery, making it more appealing to the people it hopes will buy one.

Sources indicate that A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform. Yes, that really is what it's called. Up front, the motor, inverter, and reduction gears share a single compact assembly that sends 90 horsepower and 98 pound-feet (133 Nm) to the front wheels. Suzuki says it chose LFP for safety and longevity, but it hasn’t given the European car a range or charging figure yet.

Recent findings suggest that the Ignis EV has a very tight 29.5-foot (9-meter) turning circle. Its overhangs are tiny, giving it a wheel-at-each-corner stance that looks unique while maximizing available interior room. The LED signatures at both ends take their shape from digital numerals, and the dark pillars give the roof a floating look.

Sources indicate that inside, a curve runs from the dashboard into the doors, with a wide display and a ceramic-inspired storage tray across the dash. Suzuki President Toshihiro Suzuki credits the company’s decades of building Japanese mini vehicles for its ability to provide a genuinely usable cabin in such a small footprint.

For decades, European brands had most of this business to themselves. If you wanted an inexpensive car that could squeeze down a narrow street, Fiat would happily sell you a Panda, Renault a Twingo and Volkswagen an Up. Chinese automakers see an opening as those buyers go electric.

Leapmotor brought the T03 to Europe through its partnership with Stellantis, while BYD adapted its Chinese-market Seagull for Europe and called it the Dolphin Surf. Driving the latter, what stood out to me was how well it drove, how little felt cheap, and how much kit it had for its sub-€20,000 starting price.

It has been revealed that by the time the Ignis arrives next year, European buyers will have had plenty of practice shopping for small EVs. Renault has revived both the 5 and the Twingo as electric cars, and there’s also the related Dacia Spring. Volkswagen has the ID. Polo, Cupra has the Raval, and Skoda has the Epiq, and there definitely seems to be demand for them. In September, a major VW dealer group reported more than 30,000 orders for the ID. Polo and a waiting list stretching to ten months.

That leaves one substantial question for the little Suzuki. What will it cost? Consider the redesigned Dacia Spring. Dacia moved production from China to Slovenia, shared the electric Twingo’s underpinnings, and produced a car that starts at €17,900 in Italy. It gets up to 155 miles (250 kilometers) of WLTP range from a battery only slightly larger than the one in the Ignis.

Narrowed Focus: 1997 Toyota Camry LE Tested

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that over 3,000,000 sold!
  • That won’t change as Toyota introduces its fourth-­generation Camry in Sep­tember, and neither will the mix of virtues that make this model a favorite.
  • See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 21014.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that over 3,000,000 sold! Call it the McCamry. Along with the Ford Taurus and the Honda Accord, this Toyota is right at the top of the list when Amer­ican families go new-car shopping, and right at the top of the ratings in our last family-sedan comparison test (November 1995). Since its introduction here in 1983, Toyota has diligently smoothed up, slicked up, and suaved up the Camry till the only remaining awkwardness is the unlikely spelling of its name.

That won’t change as Toyota introduces its fourth-­generation Camry in Sep­tember, and neither will the mix of virtues that make this model a favorite. We’re talking refinement of the Camry theme, not reinvention. In fact, the basic platform and powertrain carry on, though engineering improvements seem to touch every part of the car. It’s slightly bigger in each exterior dimension—0.7 inch longer, 0.4 inch wider, 2.1 inches longer in wheelbase; the same four­-cylinder and V-6 engines are modestly more powerful (up 8 hp in the four, up 6 hp in the V-6); and the interior has been upgraded to meet all the safety standards scheduled in the next few years, including the 1997 side-impact and 1999 head-­impact requirements. The aerodynamic drag coefficient has been improved to 0.30, from 0.33.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 21014.

Toyota is, however, tightening the Camry’s focus. It’s available only as a four-door now in three trim levels: CE, LE, and XLE. Gone is the coupe, which won over just five percent of Camry buyers. Gone, too, is the station wagon, a shape that convinced only three per­cent of Camry buyers in its losing battle against the tide of minivans. (Production of a Camry-based minivan begins next spring.).

It has been revealed that in the past, we’ve joked that the Camry’s personality is one of aggressive bland­ness. Unlike the frisky feeling of the Accord and the athletic tautness of the Dodge Intrepid, both of which come through loud and clear before you’ve driven to the first corner, the Camry’s subtlety grows on you over time. It’s smoother, softer, quieter than the others, less com­municative, less mechanical. Instead of talking to you in the very pleasant way of those others, it’s the silent type that, you soon notice, goes expertly about its job.

Sources indicate that in this newly introduced Camry, Toyota sharpened the expertise without changing the per­sonality. It’s still a car that’s light to the touch: easy to steer, easy to brake. The ride is commendably free of harshness, thanks in part to mounting the suspension on isolated crossmembers front and rear. The four­-cylinder version, with its 195/70SR-14 tires, rides very smoothly and ignores almost completely the road textures that create so much droning in sporting cars. The V-6s come with 205/65HR-15s on six­-inch-wide wheels. These tires are noticeably harsher and noisier than those on the four-cylinder cars, though road nose is still quite reasonable when compared with other cars in this class. Road grip and handling predictability are well above the minimums we’d set for family cars.

See all results for used 1997 Toyota Camry for sale near 21014.

The Camry V-6 has been one of the top performers in this class. The 1997 model gains six horsepower (now 194 hp at the same 5200 rpm as the previous peak), gets shorter final-drive gearing (3.93 versus 3.43), and weighs about the same as last year’s smaller car. Another performance plus: A manual transmission has returned to the V-6 lineup, available only on CE models. How­ever, our LE V-6 auto­matic was no quicker than the last LE V-6 we tested, managing 0 to 60 mph in 8.3 seconds. Expect the five-speed to trim that by about four-tenths.

On the road, the automatic’s eagerness to change down a gear or two when you press the pedal, even slightly, and the seamless smoothness of those changes give this car quick reflexes in traffic. The engine revs with the hushed moan of a Lexus. This year, traction control is optional on LE and XLE V-6 models. When it comes to powertrain pleasures, the Camry is world-class.

It has been revealed that still, it’s the more subtle details of pas­senger accommodation that make this Toyota a family favorite. In the previous­-generation Camry, our comparison tests show two adults fit in the back seat more comfortably than in some other brands up to 10 inches longer. We expect this Camry advantage to widen fractionally in this new model because both legroom and head­room in back are increased by a half-inch. Although the Camry is wider on the out­side, energy-absorbing padding to protect in side impacts takes up the extra space and, in certain spots, a little more. The Camry still has pockets in the front doors, unlike the Taurus, which sacrificed them for crash-protection equipment.

Those who wish to maximize rear-seat space should think twice about opting for power front seats (standard equipment on the top-of-the-line XLE). The manual­adjust buckets have excellent toeroom under them, which the power adjuster interrupts with a transverse bar. Tall folks won’t like that.

As in most modern sedans, the Camry has fold-forward rear seatbacks split one­-third and two-thirds, allowing the cargo compartment to be extended into the pas­senger area. Here’s another think-twice: Camrys equipped with the optional child seat—it’s built into the two-thirds section of the rear seat—have that section fixed in place, ruling out all but a narrow passage into the trunk.

According to recent reports, at the rear, the trunklid opens wider and lower than before. Space inside, however, is a bit less in the new body—14.1 cubic feet versus 14.8 before. And the new car still has the conventional trunk hinges with the sickle arms that swing down into your luggage when the lid is closed.

Sources indicate that conventional is the right description for the new instrument panel, certainly more conventional than the old one, which tried to visually compartmentalize the cockpit by emphasizing a huge black field in front of the driver. That was the good part. The bad part was the deemphasized and totally boring padding it left for the passenger’s amusement. Now the all-new panel stretches its padding across the inte­rior in an equal-opportunity gesture that makes the interior seem brighter and wider. The glove box is 29 percent larger. The audio controls were raised to a mid­dash height, making them easy to see and reach. The climate controls have changed over to the increasingly common turn-to-adjust knobs. They’re large enough, and so obvious in their workings, that they are easy to operate in their less prominent location. The Camry continues to position its ignition switch in the dash where you can readily see it, instead of hiding it on the side of the steering column.

Toyota has proven itself to be the master of those little conveniences that add up to an exceptionally pleasing car. In this latest Camry we see more clever trade-offs as the engineers cut costs, reduce weight, and usually end up serving the customer better, too. For example, the new front bumper cuts the part count nearly in half and saves weight, yet it increases protec­tion to 5 mph from 2.5. Inside, the seats recline in stepless increments now, and the buckets’ height adjusters use a single knob instead of two. Both of these changes cut costs, Toyota says. We say they make the car better, too. Models that previously would have had retracting antennas now have the antenna screened on the rear glass, saving weight and cost. The new Bosch anti-lock brake system weighs half as much as the old one.

Sources indicate that still, not every cost saver is a benefit. The LCD odometer is simply gray num­bers on a gray field, making it less visible than the glowing digits in competitors like the Chrysler Cirrus and the Dodge Stratus. And the fresh one-piece front-bumper cover now incorporates the grille into its overtly ordinary Rubbermaid-looking façade.

There’s been much speculation in the automotive-trade press about a possible price cut. Don’t hold your breath. Sales of the old Camry hit records earlier this year with no apparent price cutting. Were there sweeteners for the dealer? Sure, but other brands had them, too. Toyota knows all the tricks for selling cars without collapsing its price structure-tricks, we think, that mostly won’t be needed to move this shrewdly updated Camry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Suzuki offered a first look at the all-new Ignis, its first compact EV designed specifically for global markets.
  • The first-generation Ignis went on sale back in 2000 as a three- and five-door hatchback, and in 2016, Suzuki reintroduced it as a compact crossover.
  • It has been revealed that after discontinuing the gas-powered version just last year, Suzuki is now bringing the Ignis back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Suzuki offered a first look at the all-new Ignis, its first compact EV designed specifically for global markets.

The first-generation Ignis went on sale back in 2000 as a three- and five-door hatchback, and in 2016, Suzuki reintroduced it as a compact crossover.

It has been revealed that after discontinuing the gas-powered version just last year, Suzuki is now bringing the Ignis back. This time, as a fully electric compact EV.

Suzuki revealed the all-new Ignis EV on Wednesday, deeming it the brand’s “first compact EV for global markets.”.

The electric city car is based on the original Ignis and clearly draws inspiration from the e Sky, Suzuki’s first kei EV that debuted last month in Japan.

Industry observers note that unlike the e Sky, the new Ignis EV is designed for global markets, including Europe. Suzuki stated the Ignis was developed under the concept of “Easy to Switch,” which, as you can guess, means it’s designed to make it easy for drivers to switch from a gas-powered car to electric.

To ensure it can handle urban areas and winding roads in Europe and other regions, Suzuki put the electric city car through “extensive testing” on public roads.

Suzuki fine-tuned the chassis and power delivery specifically for the different road conditions and needs of drivers in major global markets.

The global Ignis EV is also slightly larger than the e Sky, measuring 3,570 mm long, 1,565 mm wide, and 1,635 mm tall, with a 2,460 mm wheelbase.

It’s built on the same dedicated “HEARTECT-e” EV platform as the e Sky, with a single electric motor that delivers 90 hp (67 kW) and 98 lb-ft (133 Nm) of torque.

It has been revealed that the Ignis also uses the same 26 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery as the e SKY. However, Suzuki hasn’t revealed driving range figures yet. Suzuki didn’t specify, but the LFP battery pack used in the e SKY is supplied by BYD’s battery unit to keep costs down.

According to Suzuki, the e SKY for Japan offers a WLTC driving range of up to 310 km (192 miles) and a “class-leading” AC energy consumption rating of 97 Wh/km.

Inside, the new Suzuki Ignis EV adopts a similar setup to the e Sky with a space-maximizing four-seat layout and a wide infotainment display.

According to recent reports, great to have a small car option like this. Let us hope it reaches open global markets at a price similar to the e SKY. That is about the price of the BYD Seagull in Australia today (US13-14k). Unfortunately the Seagull is growing in size so it would be good to have the option of this small Suzuki.

It seems likely it will be much more expensive in Europe as all EVs are.

In a recent development, suzuki will launch the Ignis in Europe and other markets starting in summer 2027. Prices have yet to be revealed, but the Ignis will enter an increasingly competitive segment of entry-level compact EVs, including the Renault Twingo, BYD Dolphin Surf, and Honda Super-N.

In Japan, Suzuki’s e SKY undercuts much of the competition with prices starting at just ¥2,120,000 ($13,500).

According to recent reports, for context, the Renault Twingo E-Tech starts at under €19,490 ($21,500) in Europe and £14,745 in the UK. BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at around €22,990 ($25,500) and £18,675 ($24,500) in the UK, while the Honda Super-N starts at £18,995 ($25,000) in the UK.

Which compact EV would you drive? Let us know in the comments. Unfortunately, none of them will be coming to the US.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic.
  • In a recent development, this fresh mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.
  • As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star.

Industry observers note that split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

In a recent development, this fresh mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an problem for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming update, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

10 Fighting Games That Totally Reinvent Themselves Halfway Through

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I am a full-time fighting game enthusiast.
  • Industry observers note that having played countless fighting games over the years, a handful stand out for how dramatically they shift their rules, mechanics, or entire structure mid-match, mid-mode, or halfway through a campaign.
  • In a recent development, I grew up alongside Goku and his friends, sinking hundreds of hours into every Dragon Ball game on the PlayStation 2 and PS4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I am a full-time fighting game enthusiast. I thrive on those intense, white-knuckle matches that push my skills to the limit—even when I have to retry a tough fight over and over. Honestly, half the magic lies in that process of adapting until you finally break through the wall. Beyond pure mechanics, though, I have a special soft spot for titles that refuse to stay boxed in, introducing fresh rules and systems as you progress until they practically reinvent themselves halfway through.

Industry observers note that having played countless fighting games over the years, a handful stand out for how dramatically they shift their rules, mechanics, or entire structure mid-match, mid-mode, or halfway through a campaign. They genuinely caught me off guard when I first played them, keeping the experience fresh instead of letting it settle into a predictable loop. Here are 10 fighting games that pull off that kind of reinvention, ranked from the cleverest twists to the most radical genre-bending shifts.

In a recent development, I grew up alongside Goku and his friends, sinking hundreds of hours into every Dragon Ball game on the PlayStation 2 and PS4. Naturally, I nearly teared up with excitement when Dragon Ball: Sparking! ZERO was unveiled—and once I finally got my hands on it, the combat immediately won me over, recapturing the spirit of Dragon Ball Z: Budokai Tenkaichi 3 with sharper visuals and an expanded roster.

As I dove deeper into its Episode Battle campaign, however, I realized it wasn't just retreading familiar manga and anime arcs. By fulfilling specific hidden objectives mid-fight—like defeating an opponent within a strict time limit or making an unexpected choice—you unlock Sparking! Episodes, which act as full-fledged "What If?" timelines that rewrite the rest of that character's campaign. Seeing the story branch off into uncharted territory made clearing the main mode feel far more exciting than simply replaying the same plot beats we all know by heart.

It has been revealed that I have been a die-hard fan of Jin Kazama's saga ever since I first booted up Tekken 3 on the original PlayStation, and I've played nearly every entry since—including Tekken 7 on PS4 (following its 2015 arcade debut). Beyond bringing an expanded roster and memorable newcomers to the table, it also shook up the formula halfway through its main story campaign to give the climax far more dramatic weight.

According to recent reports, throughout the first half of The Mishima Saga, the game sticks to the series' classic blueprint: straightforward one-on-one bouts fought under standard Tekken rules. Once Heihachi reclaims the Mishima Zaibatsu in the second half, though, the campaign throws traditional tournament rules out the window in favor of boss encounters featuring super armor phases, special EX and Rage meters, health regeneration, and mid-fight Quick-Time Events that turn battles into cinematic spectacles. Those mechanics completely changed how I approached the late-game fights, forcing me to play much more defensively so I wouldn't enter the next phase with a depleted health bar.

Mortal Kombat is another legendary franchise that has delivered decades of over-the-top violence, though narrative fatigue and identity issues eventually pushed NetherRealm Studios to hit the reset button with Mortal Kombat 1.

Industry observers note that I placed Mortal Kombat 1 here because of how dramatically it flips both its narrative tone and its opponent design in the final stretch of its Story Mode. Across the first 14 chapters, the campaign presents a relatively grounded reboot centered on martial arts tournaments and political intrigue within Liu Kang's Fresh Era.

Once the story reaches its climax at the Pyramid of Argus, however, the multiverse blows wide open and pits you against procedurally generated hybrid fighters that mash up the appearances, special moves, and Fatalities of two different characters into one. Facing off against unpredictable fusions completely changes how you read opponents on the fly, turning the finale into a chaotic, anything-goes brawl.

Sources indicate that another absolute favorite from my old PS2 days—and one I would love to see get a proper remake or sequel—is Def Jam: Fight for NY. It let you build your own custom brawler and drop straight into a gritty turf war packed with betrayals, brutal environmental knockouts, and some of the biggest hip-hop icons of the era.

In a recent development, what really hooked me in its Story Mode was how your moveset evolves halfway through the climb. You start by creating your fighter and picking a single base discipline from five options: Martial Arts, Wrestling, Submissions, Kickboxing, or Streetfighting. Later on, by training at Stapleton Athletics gym, you unlock the ability to buy and fuse up to three distinct fighting styles onto your character—completely rewriting your combo strings, counters, and Blazin' finishers depending on the exact styles you combine.

You can't talk about standout modern fighting games without bringing up Street Fighter 6, a title I have easily poured dozens of hours into. Much like the other entries on this list, its single-player journey gradually reinvents itself into something far wilder than its opening hours suggest.

Recent findings suggest that early on in World Tour, you control a rookie avatar roaming Metro City with a bare-bones moveset while learning the fundamentals of the Drive System. Once you travel to Nayshall and start training under multiple Masters from the main roster, however, the mode opens up into a full-blown hybrid moveset sandbox. Before long, you can mix and match special moves from completely incompatible archetypes—pairing Ryu's Hadoken with Zangief's Spinning Piledriver and Chun-Li's kicks—exclusively within World Tour and the Battle Hub.

Industry observers note that unlike most games on this list, Nidhogg reinvents its genre dynamically in the middle of every single match. Each bout begins in the center of the stage as a tense, minimalist one-on-one fencing duel where spacing, blade height, and timely disarms mean everything.

Sources indicate that the moment one player scores a kill, though, the game instantly mutates from a methodical duel into a frantic obstacle-course platformer. The winner has to sprint across multiple screens toward their goal while the defeated player repeatedly respawns ahead to stop them using any dirty trick available—from dive kicks to throwing their sword—flipping attacker and defender roles back and forth until someone finally reaches the end to be devoured by the giant Nidhogg worm.

As we climb closer to the top spot, the mid-game transformations become much more drastic. At its core, For Honor is built around its Art of Battle directional guard system, demanding careful reads in close-quarters melee duels—and in its large-scale Breach mode, the first two phases revolve around escorting or halting a battering ram.

Industry observers note that introduced with the Marching Fire expansion in October 2018, Breach completely changes its structure once the ram breaks through both gates. At that point, the ram disappears and the match transforms into an asymmetrical raid with limited respawn tickets, forcing the attacking team to coordinate and take down an AI-controlled Commander with massive health and area-of-effect attacks while defenders fight to keep him alive—turning tactical skirmishes into a high-stakes team raid.

Originally released in arcades in 1996 before finally reaching modern consoles and PC in 2022 via Capcom Fighting Collection, although it's one of those games from the Japanese firm that desperately needs a remake. Red Earth (known as Warzard in Japan) took a wildly unconventional approach to the genre. Rather than pitting you against a traditional lineup of rival fighters, it built its main Quest Mode around full-fledged RPG progression.

Recent findings suggest that it kicks off like a classic Capcom 2D fighter with a striking dark-fantasy aesthetic, letting you choose from four heroes, before quickly shifting into a boss-rush RPG. As you clear battles, your character earns experience, levels up, unlocks newly introduced special moves, and picks up elemental orbs and weapons off the ground to survive multi-phase encounters against towering monsters that mutate and change their attack patterns mid-fight.

It has been revealed that super Smash Bros. Brawl remains a beloved favorite for many fans, and its main campaign pulled off a full-blown genre switch in its second act. Throughout the first half of The Subspace Emissary, the mode plays like a linear, side-scrolling beat 'em up broken into distinct stages with rotating pairs of heroes—a straightforward formula I genuinely enjoyed.

However, once the roster finally unites in Subspace and suffers a crushing defeat at the hands of Tabuu, the entire mode transforms into The Great Maze. Suddenly, those linear stages give way to a massive, interconnected, non-linear Metroidvania-style map where you command the entire unlocked roster, rescue captured trophies, and backtrack through merged zones to rematch bosses—a sudden shift in structure that completely caught me off guard back in the day.

According to recent reports, when it comes to fighting games that radically reinvent themselves halfway through, Soulcalibur III takes the crown. On the surface, it serves as the direct follow-up to Soulcalibur II's fast-paced, 3D weapon-based combat built around smooth 8-Way Run movement—familiar territory for anyone who loved the series on PlayStation 2.

Sources indicate that inside its signature Chronicles of the Sword campaign, however, the game fuses traditional one-on-one weapon duels with a real-time strategy game. You command squads across a tactical map, capture strongholds, and level up custom-built units—and by the second half of the campaign, early small-scale skirmishes escalate into complex, multi-front sieges against iconic series veterans and high-level bosses that test both your strategic planning and your blade skills.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that changes in mood later in life may offer vital clues about what is happening inside the brain, even before problems with memory or thinking become noticeable.
  • Sources indicate that the study, published in JNeurosci, was conducted by Teodora Markova of Brandeis University and her colleagues.
  • Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Worsening Depression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that changes in mood later in life may offer vital clues about what is happening inside the brain, even before problems with memory or thinking become noticeable. Latest research suggests that the buildup of tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, may contribute to worsening depressive symptoms in older adults.

Sources indicate that the study, published in JNeurosci, was conducted by Teodora Markova of Brandeis University and her colleagues. The team investigated how tau levels relate to depression during normal aging and in people experiencing the cognitive (memory, attention, and thinking) difficulties associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Worsening Depression.

Industry observers note that to investigate this connection, researchers analyzed information from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, a research project that tracks changes in brain health over time. The data included older men and women, some with cognitive difficulties and others whose memory and thinking abilities remained intact.

Industry observers note that participants underwent multiple brain scans designed to detect tau accumulation and completed questionnaires assessing depressive symptoms at different points during the study. This allowed researchers to examine how changes in tau levels corresponded with changes in mood over time.

In a recent development, among participants with normal cognitive abilities, the researchers discovered a striking pattern. Those whose tau levels increased more rapidly also tended to experience a faster rise in depressive symptoms. Higher tau levels also helped predict more severe depressive symptoms in these individuals.

Recent findings suggest that the results suggest that tau may begin influencing mood before measurable cognitive problems emerge. However, the same relationships were not observed among participants who already had mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease.

Could Depression Reveal Early Brain Changes?

The findings suggest that tau accumulation during the early stages of brain aging may contribute to the development or worsening of depression. They also raise the possibility that changes in mood could provide useful information about brain health before memory loss becomes apparent.

Researchers believe that following depressive symptoms over time, alongside other assessments, could eventually help identify older adults who may be at greater risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases. However, additional research is needed to establish whether these early changes in mood can reliably predict future cognitive decline.

Markova emphasized the importance of studying these relationships over longer periods, particularly as some participants develop more noticeable depression or begin experiencing cognitive difficulties.

"Future work can continue to track how participants' tau levels and depression symptoms evolve over longer periods of time, particularly as some develop cognitive impairment or more clinically significant levels of depression. Continuing to follow these trajectories, observing how early mood changes relate to later clinical outcomes, and establishing relationships with other methods tracking the development of Alzheimer's disease will provide more clarity on methods to determine which individuals may be at an increased risk.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ionna, the EV charging network that ranked first in J.D. Power’s latest public charging satisfaction survey, has slashed prices at its stations across the country for Thanksgiving weekend.

Recent findings suggest that the firm, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States. That’s a 50% discount, and drivers don’t have to do anything special to get it—just plug in and pay, either through the automaker’s official smartphone app, the on-site payment terminals, or the Presto app for Tesla owners who want to enjoy the Autocharge function.

In a recent development, for long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a substantial difference. A single 50-kilowatt-hour session that used to cost $20 will now be just $10 plus tax, but seeing how many people are traveling across the country these days, multiple sessions will be necessary, driving the cost savings even further.

And it’s not like the cost reduction comes with any strings attached. Ionna uses 400-kilowatt chargers from Alpitronic exclusively, so there’s plenty of wiggle room for even the most power-hungry EVs out there. What’s more, many stalls have dual cords for each port, with a CCS connector and a NACS connector, so charging adapters aren’t needed at most locations.

Separately, Ionna has discounts for several automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, BMW, General Motors, and Stellantis.

It has been revealed that the charging operator installed its first stalls in 2024, and it has wasted no time expanding its footprint quickly. On its second anniversary, Ionna celebrated by opening its 100th site, and the company now has 229 sites and nearly 1,900 ports nationwide, according to the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC). Still, the charging network is not slowing down, with dozens of locations under construction and aims to introduce 500-kW chargers in the near future.

According to recent reports, most EV brands support Plug & Charge at Ionna, with Tesla recently getting Autocharge functionality through a third-party smartphone application. Ionna itself doesn’t have a smartphone app, instead relying on automakers and third-party apps to integrate its locations. So far, this approach has turned out to be quite successful, with J.D. Power’s latest public charging survey putting the operator first, ahead of Tesla and the rest of the competition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, very much when we expected it, Blizzard has officially revealed Diablo 4’s next major expansion at The Game Awards. Lord of Hatred delivers a newly introduced campaign that continues the mainline story, picking up from where Vessel of Hatred left off. Mephisto, the eponymous Lord of Hatred, has seemingly finally escaped imprisonment to rule over Sanctuary.

Lord of Hatred is the second Diablo 4 expansion, and it will be available on PC, PS5, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X/S on April 28.

It has been revealed that it’s always a big deal when we get a newly introduced Diablo expansion, especially for a game as starved of fresh (major) content as Diablo 4 has been. But perhaps the biggest piece of news out of the Lord of Hatred reveal is that the expansion is bringing not one, but two new classes to the game.

The first of which is The Paladin, whereas the second is being kept under wraps. Even more surprising is that The Paladin is playable right now for anyone who pre-purchases the expansion. This is a well-timed shadow drop, especially given that Diablo 4’s latest season has just kicked off.

The expansion adds a fresh region to the world: Skovos, which is where the events of the new campaign will be taking place. This is the first time Skovos has been in a Diablo game. The region is of major significance to the world and lore of the series, as it is the birthplace of the firstborn, home of Lilith and Inaruis.

Lord of Hatred brings a decent number of major systems to Diablo 4. The endgame is getting a massive overhaul, headlined by the fresh War Prepares feature. Through this, you can effectively design your own endgame grind, creating challenges based on the activities you like and earning rewards along the way.

Endgame activities now also feature their own skill trees, which can be progressed through by creating War Intends for your character featuring each activity. The new endgame activity, Echoing Hatred, is something of horde mode where you must defend against unrelenting waves of enemies.

None of that matters without loot, of course, and the upcoming expansion is bringing back the Horadric Cube, and adding set bonuses using the Talisman system. The long-awaited and highly-requested Loot Filter is also coming to the game with the release of the expansion.

Industry observers note that beyond itemisation, each class’ skill tree will grow with upcoming bonus skill variants. In fact, the entire skill system is being reworked for all classes - though details are a little sparse at the moment.

You can also expect the level cap to go up, which is very likely necessary to fit all the new skills and various systems. Blizzard offered a deep dive into the new Paladin class, which you see on the official blog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hyundai’s latest IONIQ 3 checks all the boxes as an affordable EV: it offers over 300 miles of range, a practical interior, and Hyundai’s new Pleos infotainment system. So, will Hyundai bring it to the US?

The Hyundai IONIQ 3 is now on sale across Europe and the UK as a smaller sibling to the IONIQ 5, positioned between the Inster EV and Hyundai Kona Electric.

According to recent reports, although it’s part of the IONIQ sub-brand, the IONIQ 3 features a latest “Aero Hatch” design. The new look “reimagines the compact EV silhouette,” Hyundai said, designed to optimize efficiency and interior space.

The response so far has been “extraordinary,” Ashley Andrew, president of Hyundai Motor UK, mentioned after launching the IONIQ 3 last month.

According to Andrew, the compact EV received “more customers registering their interest before launch than any fresh Hyundai we’ve introduced in the UK,” and that’s including gas-powered and electric vehicles.

The first reviews of the IONIQ 3 have been overwhelmingly positive, highlighting its efficiency, practical interior, and affordable price tag.

Update 11/25/2026: A Hyundai spokesperson told Electrek that “it’s likely that the IONIQ 3 that was apparently spotted in the US recently was the same unit that was brought in for World Car of the Year’s annual test days” held in Pasadena, California.

It looks like the IONIQ 3 will be another affordable, practical EV the US will miss out on.

A post shared by KindelAuto (@kindelauto).

The update from Hyundai comes after the IONIQ 3 was recently captured driving on public US roads, raising speculation, or perhaps hope, that it will come to the States after all.

The model spotted in the images from KindelAuto is the IONIQ 3 N Line, a sportier, higher-priced trim.

While it’s among the first sightings in the US, we have seen several Hyundai Motor Group electric vehicles testing in the US that are still not available and likely won’t ever be, such as Kia’s EV5 SUV and PV5 van.

The IONIQ 3 is built at Hyundai Motor’s Izmit, Turkey, plant and is specifically designed for European drivers.

In a recent development, in Europe and the UK, Hyundai offers the IONIQ 3 with two battery packs: 42 kWh and 61 kWh. The base IONIQ 3 Advance trim with the 42 kWh battery starts at £18,495 ($25,000) OTR and offers up to 213 miles of WLTP range. That’s including the UK’s £3,750 Electric Car Grant.

In a recent development, the IONIQ 3 Advance with the 61 kWh battery starts at £21,995 ($29,000) and offers a “class-leading” WLTP range of up to 308 miles. That also includes the UK government ECG grant.

Measuring 4,155 mm (163.5″) long, 1,800 mm (70.9″) wide, and 1,505 mm (59.3″) high, with a wheelbase of 2,680 mm (105.5″), Hyundai’s electric hatch is even smaller than the Kia EV3 and Volkswagen ID.3.

The IONIQ 3 is also Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe equipped with its new Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Hyundai’s upcoming system is more like using a smartphone. It’s based on the Android Automotive OS with apps and customizable screens, similar to Tesla models. It’s available in the IONIQ 3 with a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

It has been revealed that unlike the larger IONIQ 5, the IONIQ 3 uses a 400V architecture. However, the 42 kWh battery can still recharge from 10% to 80% in about 29 minutes. The 61 kWh battery takes around 30 minutes.

In Germany and other European markets, Hyundai’s compact IONIQ 3 starts at about €28,950 ($33,000).

While Hyundai currently has no looks to bring the IONIQ 3 to the US, it does sell the IONIQ 5, built at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America outside Savannah, GA, alongside the three-row IONIQ 9.

Starting at about $35,000, Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 has remained among the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside of the Tesla Model Y and Model 3.

In fact, Hyundai was just named the “Best Electric Vehicle Brand” by US News & World Report for the first time for 2027.

Too bad Tesla refuses to build something like this. Ford could also make a similar car and bring back the Focus nameplate. I don't understand their management decisions.

Hyundai’s sister organization, Kia, also released the 2027 EV3, which is now on sale starting at just $29,890 in the US.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.
  • Recent findings suggest that to make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are right now training them to do various tasks.
  • Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.

Recent findings suggest that to make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are right now training them to do various tasks. Volvo said that it aims to support employees in repetitive and “ergonomically challenging work,” and it’s not the only car manufacturer that’s leaning towards replacing humans with robots.

Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories.

In a recent development, while fixed robotic arms have been a staple of automotive factories for decades, some brands are now investing a lot of time and money in artificial intelligence-powered robots that can do tasks where components don’t always land in the same exact spot. So-called pick-and-place jobs are gradually being taken over by robots, with Tesla, General Motors, Ford, and Rivian slowly but surely filling their factories with complex robots.

Volvo is no different, and while the first humanoids shipped to the tech giant’s plant in Ghent are only being trained right now, they’ll gradually start going to work in real conditions starting in mid 2027, the Swedish manufacturer said.

It has been revealed that presently, Volvo Cars is using imitation learning to teach the robot how to pick up and place certain components into two fixtures with high precision. Through the learning process, the team will gradually make the work more challenging, adding multiple parts, moving around the production area, and interacting with the plant’s automated systems.

“Aeon’s humanoid design means it can fit into our production as it is today, alongside our teams and existing automation,” states Magnus Nilsson, Chief Manufacturing Officer at Volvo Cars. “Our aim is for humanoid robots to take on some of the most physically demanding tasks and help make work more ergonomic for our people.”.

It has been revealed that the robot chosen by Volvo looks like a human, but it doesn’t have feet. Instead, the 5.4-foot (1.65-meter) robot moves on wheels and is capable of reaching up to 5.3 miles per hour (8.6 kilometers per hour). It weighs 132 pounds (60 kilograms) and can carry up to 22 lbs (10 kg). Several cameras and sensors are used to capture its surroundings and handle parts with precision.

Tech Report: Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game.
  • Sources indicate that the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • In a recent development, from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

Sources indicate that the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

In a recent development, from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

Sources indicate that it makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

In a recent development, thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

According to recent reports, in terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

Recent findings suggest that between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make fresh, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

#168154. Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures

Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most materials simply react when something pushes, pulls, or bends them.
  • Recent findings suggest that everyday materials such as metal, concrete, glass, and rubber are generally considered passive.
  • Recent findings suggest that active matter works differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most materials simply react when something pushes, pulls, or bends them. But a very different category of matter can draw on its own energy to change shape and respond to outside forces in surprising ways. Known as active matter, these unusual materials are attracting growing scientific interest. Now, physicists from the universities of Amsterdam, Fresh South Wales, and Cambridge have uncovered remarkable new behaviors that could change how future machines and robots are designed.

Recent findings suggest that everyday materials such as metal, concrete, glass, and rubber are generally considered passive. They can stretch, bend, shift, or change shape when forces act on them, but the energy needed to produce those changes comes from outside the material.

Recent findings suggest that active matter works differently. It contains an internal source of energy that allows it to respond to its surroundings in ways ordinary materials cannot. Many examples occur naturally in living systems. A flock of birds, for instance, can move together as a coordinated group, adjusting its behavior in response to wind, changes in the landscape, available food, or a suitable place to rest.

Scientists can also recreate some of these remarkable properties in the laboratory. Researchers from the University of Amsterdam (The Netherlands), the University of Cambridge (UK), and the University of Latest South Wales (Sydney, Australia) have spent several years developing active materials from surprisingly simple components, including miniature motors, rods, and rubber bands. Their experiments have revealed unusual mechanical behaviors with potentially valuable applications, leading to two recently accepted scientific papers.

Scientists Create Materials That Can Crawl, Walk, and Dig.

One of the discoveries involves two familiar mechanical behaviors known as buckling and snapping.

According to recent reports, imagine squeezing a paper ticket between your fingers. As the pressure increases, the ticket becomes unstable and bends to one side. If you then press against the curved surface, it initially pushes back before suddenly flipping in the opposite direction.

This is how ordinary passive materials behave. External forces supply the energy needed for the ticket to buckle and snap, and each action occurs only once in response to the applied force.

The researchers discovered that adding internal activity can fundamentally transform this behavior. They assembled a series of connected rods into a flexible chain, placing small motors at the joints where neighboring rods meet. These motors created interactions that were not symmetrical. Moving one rod could affect its neighbor in a different way than moving that neighbor would affect the original rod (by rotating over a different angle, for example).

According to recent reports, the result was striking. When external forces acted on these active chains, they still bent and snapped, but the movement no longer had to end after a single event. Instead, the structures could repeatedly buckle and snap, producing ongoing oscillations.

Industry observers note that the underlying physics involves a transformation of the system's critical point, where snapping normally takes place, into what researchers call a critical exceptional point. This unusual behavior makes it possible for the chains to generate movements resembling crawling, walking, and even digging.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, with Sami Al-Izzi of the University of New South Wales and Yao Du of the University of Amsterdam serving as joint first authors. One of the team's buckling chains was also featured on the journal's cover.

Beyond revealing unexpected physics, the discovery points toward a promising approach to building materials capable of performing multiple tasks autonomously. Such structures could be especially useful in flexible, "soft" robots, potentially allowing their bodies to produce complex movements without relying on a centralized control system.

Active Matter Challenges a Fundamental Engineering Principle.

A separate investigation by the same international research team uncovered another surprising property of active materials, this time challenging a principle widely used in engineering.

Whether designing large bridges or tiny nanomechanical devices, engineers depend on established rules that connect the properties of individual components to the behavior of an entire structure.

One such rule is Le Chatelier's Principle. In the mechanical context described by the researchers, it suggests that changes made to individual parts of a system should produce corresponding changes in the overall structure. For example, making a structure's individual components stiffer would generally be expected to increase the stiffness of the entire assembly.

Industry observers note that but the researchers found that active matter does not always follow this expectation. In some cases, increasing the activity of individual components can actually reduce the activity of the material as a whole.

To investigate this counterintuitive effect, the scientists built another structure using motors and rods. Rather than arranging the components in a chain, they connected them into a flat, two-dimensional network resembling a lattice. They then examined how the elastic behavior of the entire structure changed depending on the properties of its individual elements.

Their experiments revealed that the overall response depended on more than simply how active each component was. What mattered was whether the active elements formed connected pathways capable of transmitting mechanical responses throughout the structure.

Why More Activity Can Produce Less Response.

The researchers identified a process called percolation as the key to understanding this unexpected behavior.

It has been revealed that A useful comparison is the movement of water through ground coffee. If the coffee grounds are packed too tightly, water cannot easily travel through the entire layer. The arrangement of the grounds determines whether the water can find a continuous path.

It has been revealed that something similar happens inside active materials. If too many of the interconnected components have relatively low activity, they can prevent elastic responses from spreading through the structure. Even when other components are extremely active, their influence may not extend across the entire material.

Industry observers note that this explains why making some parts more active does not necessarily produce a more active structure overall. The way the components are connected and distributed can be just as important as their individual properties.

The second study, led by first author Jack Binysh from Corentin Coulais's research group at the University of Amsterdam, was published in Physical Review X.

The researchers believe that this unexpected departure from Le Chatelier's Principle could have important implications for understanding and designing systems built from active microscopic structures. These include biological gels, epithelial monolayers, which are sheets of closely connected cells, and neuromorphic networks that mimic aspects of biological information processing.

Together, the findings reveal how dramatically materials can behave when their internal components actively consume energy and interact in unconventional ways. The discoveries could influence research across physics, soft matter science, mechanical engineering, the life sciences, and robotics, while opening new possibilities for creating adaptable materials and smarter robotic systems.

A Used Cybertruck Is Selling A Month Faster Than A Ford F-150

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet.
  • The data from the upcoming iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla confirmed it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027.
  • In a recent development, the Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet. It’s America’s best-selling midsize truck and has a reputation for holding its value. Or you might pick the super frugal Ford Maverick Hybrid. But the truck that beat them both was the Tesla Cybertruck.

The data from the upcoming iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla confirmed it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027. The study looked at one- to five-year-old vehicles and ranked models by how long they’d been listed before selling.

In a recent development, the Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall. The Maverick Hybrid came closest at 43.3 days, followed by the Rivian R1T at 45.2 and the F-150 Lightning at 47.4. The Tacoma came in fifth position.

Industry observers note that the gap between the two electric pickups at either end of the list was even more striking. A used Chevrolet Silverado EV took 107.5 days to sell, putting it last among the 24 trucks in the study. That’s a 68-day difference between two American electric pickups. Across the wider used market, EVs averaged about 46 days to find a buyer, around nine fewer than hybrids and 15 fewer than gas vehicles.

Industry observers note that how quickly a used Cybertruck sold seems to have changed a lot since May 2024, when some sellers were cutting as much as $30,000 from their asking prices after listing their trucks for close to $200,000. By December of that year, we reported that used Cybertrucks were piling up on dealer lots, with data at the time showing they stayed for 75 days, up from 27 in May.

Sources indicate that then owners got a look at what Tesla itself would pay for a used Cybertruck trade-in. One year later, in May 2025, one owner of a $99,990 dual-motor Foundation Series truck got a trade-in estimate of $65,400 after driving it just 6,211 miles.

So even though the Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used pickup in iSeeCars’ fresh study, it didn’t report what buyers paid, so we don’t know whether owners got their asking price or had to lower it to sell.

Sources indicate that tesla will build the last Cybertrucks at the end of summer 2027, and this will reshape their used market. Elon Musk originally unveiled production would end around the middle of the year, but then extended the run to fill more orders. And if you order a Cybertruck now, the only one you can get is the $110,000 tri-motor Cyberbeast, so anyone who wants a less expensive dual-motor truck has to look for a used example.

It has been revealed that once the last latest Cybertruck is sold, I’d expect collectors and everyday truck buyers to look at used ones differently. Someone after a clean Foundation Series truck with low miles might pay a little extra for one close to home, especially since it could be months before another comes up for sale nearby.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, someone who just needs an electric pickup to tow a trailer has more options. If a used dual-motor Cybertruck costs about the same as a Ford F-150 Lightning or a Rivian R1T, I suspect that buyer will care more about mileage, condition, and how much battery warranty is left than when Tesla built its last truck.

  • Sources indicate that larian calls Divinity its most ambitious title ever, with the studio striving for a level of depth and breadth we’ve not seen before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Larian Studios has delivered what was arguably the biggest reveal of The Game Awards 2025 showcase. The Hellstone, the mysterious monolith in the desert that’s been generating a lot of speculation in the lead-up to the show was indeed teasing the studio’s next game.

According to recent reports, the Belgian developer is returning to the series it created with Divinity, a non-numbered sequel that’s designed for newly introduced and veteran players alike. The announcement was entirely cinematic, setting the tone for what looks to be the next substantial thing in the space.

Sources indicate that larian calls Divinity its most ambitious title ever, with the studio striving for a level of depth and breadth we’ve not seen before. This is the next project from the Baldur’s Gate 3 team, after all, so there’s understandably immense anticipation for it.

According to recent reports, divinity is a standalone RPG, and does not require you to have played Divinity: Original Sin, or Divinity: Original Sin 2. If you did, however, you’re going to find the journey extra special because of the continuity it offers.

“We’re ready to bring everything we’ve done previously into one place,” said founder and game director, Swen Vincke.

“This marks the beginning of something with more breadth, depth, and intimacy than anything we’ve created before. We’ve been building toward this moment ever since we took our fate into our own hands. This is the Divinity we’ve always wanted to make and you're going to have loads of fun with it.”.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, there’s precious little that’s been revealed for Divinity so far. We don’t know what platforms it’s going to be coming to, nor do we even have a release target. We do know it’s an RPG, so you can very much expect something similar to earlier games in the series, and, of course, Baldur’s Gate 3.
